records.name: Gyeonggi
records.summary:
The model student human-rights ordinance covering discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity was first enacted in 2010 by a progressive superintendent of education for Gyeonggi Province; Seoul's office adopted it in 2012 and it spread to other regional offices before the 2024–26 repeal wave.

When Seoul's metropolitan council — pushed by a campaign begun by religious and parents' coalitions in August 2022 — abolished the capital's ordinance on 26 April 2024, Gyeonggi stood among only six regional education offices still enforcing comparable ordinances, and a Gyeonggi-based teacher warned that wholesale abolition 'will bring a regression to human rights in the education sector'. The province's standing is thus origin-and-retention of student protections rather than any enforcement measure aimed at visitors.

(An earlier version of this record cited Law 21.120 as the standard breached; that law took effect in December 2019, after the denunciation.) This remains the closest Chilean analogue to a facility-misassignment incident directly encountered by a visitor: an emergency-room or inpatient visit in Bío-Bío carries a documented risk of gender-mismatched placement. Separately, Concepción's municipality dismissed the staff of its Oficina de la Diversidad y No Discriminación during the January 2025 honourary-staff cuts (~100 workers), which LGBTIQA+ organisations called a "dismantling" leaving one person in post.

records.name: RegiÃ³n de TarapacÃ¡
records.summary:
The Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled the entire trial over the killing of a transgender woman, holding that Chile's "femicide" (femicidio) offence — the strongest gendered-violence protection in the penal code — covers only "a person biologically female" and therefore the conviction could not stand as framed. The case: Yuri Pizarro, a 55-year-old trans woman whose body was found on the southern coast of the provincial capital in June 2022; her killer, Jhonatan Cañon, had been convicted at first instance to presidio perpetuo, and on the defence's nullity motion the Iquique court declared the sentence void in early October 2023. This is a named judicial finding that, in this region, the most severe legal protection available for gender-motivated violence does not extend to trans women. The annulment occurred in Tarapacá, where the Iquique court exercises jurisdiction. Tarapacá accounted for 1.56 % of the national anti-LGBTI case total in 2024, a small-share region in which a single structural finding dominates the per-capita signal.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.08 deviation. The legal framework is unchanged (Law 21.120 and the femicide article remain on the books nationally), but the regional judiciary's operative interpretation in this instance creates a concrete protection gap for a trans person who is assaulted in Tarapacá. records.summary:
Movilh's XXIV annual report (March 2026) identifies La Araucanía as the region where reported homo/transphobic cases rose most sharply in 2025 — up approximately 150 % year-on-year — during a year when the national total hit a record 3,620 documented cases (+27.1 %). The region's formal trans visibility is extremely low: only 157 people used the Gender Identity Law (21.120) for name and legal-sex rectification in its first three years, indicating a community with minimal institutional presence. Movilh interprets the pattern as the decentralisation of hate toward territories where LGBTIQ+ themes have less public debate, stating this "appears aimed at obstructing" equality work.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.07 deviation, trend-driven rather than incident-specific. There is no trans-specific Mapuche customary-law jurisdiction or documented state-implicated violence in the dossier; the indigenous-note is structural context within a region under prolonged security conflict. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), La Araucanía is 0.01 higher: Tarapacá carries a concrete judicial annulment, whereas Araucanía's finding is a statistical acceleration from a low base. Compared with Valparaíso (0.56), it is 0.09 higher despite the 150 % rise, because Araucanía's absolute share (0.72 % of national cases) remains marginal.

records.name: RegiÃ³n de Magallanes y AntÃ¡rtica Chilena
records.summary:
In 2024 a trans woman, Kenia Chacón, was the victim of an attempted femicide (femicidio frustrado) in Punta Arenas. The tribunal imposed four years of internación parcial against the five years of internación total requested by the prosecution; the victim's mother publicly denounced devaluation of the attack on the basis of her daughter's gender identity. In April 2026 the regional director of SernamEG (the national women and gender-equality service) publicly criticised the sentence as not reflecting the gravity of the attack and announced an appeal — a named institutional pushback that partially offsets the judicial under-penalisation. Magallanes also appeared among the regions with the largest percentage increases in the 2024 dataset and holds 0.96 % of the national case total.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.06 deviation. The under-sentencing for gender-motivated violence against a trans woman is a concrete traveler-relevant severity finding; the SernamEG appeal is a genuine institutional counter-signal that prevents a deeper deduction. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Magallanes is 0.02 higher: Tarapacá's Iquique court annulment voids the femicide protection entirely for trans women in that jurisdiction, whereas Magallanes applied the femicide framework but under-sentenced, and the state service is actively appealing to correct the record.

records.name: RegiÃ³n de Ãuble
records.summary:
Ñuble registered a +300 % increase in recorded homo/transphobic cases in 2024, the sharpest percentage rise of any Chilean region, though from an extremely small base: Ñuble held only 1.44 % of the national case total. La Discusión's reporting of two historic gender-identity rectification cases in Ñuble illustrates how minimal the formal trans presence is in the region. The statistical alarm is real — the fastest percentage growth in the country — but the absolute numbers remain marginal, and no region-specific legal finding, institutional incident, or enforcement failure was identified in the dossier beyond the case-volume trend. A 2026 follow-up in the same paper reports homo/transphobic attacks rising a further 16.6 % in Ñuble in 2025.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.05 deviation, driven entirely by the rate-of-change signal. Compared with Bío-Bío (0.62), which is 0.05 lower, Ñuble lacks the hospital bed-placement and diversity-office-dismantling findings that give Bío-Bío a concrete traveler-facing institutional failure. Ñuble's evidence is statistical trajectory without a named incident. Compared with La Araucanía (0.65), Ñuble is 0.02 higher: Araucanía's +150 % is in the most recent year (2025) and is accompanied by the lowest gender-identity-law uptake of any region (157 in three years), painting a more sustained picture of emerging hostility with no institutional counterweight.

records.name: RegiÃ³n de Arica y Parinacota
records.summary:
Arica y Parinacota is grouped with Tarapacá in the dossier under the heading "the northern courts' non-recognition of trans women as women," reflecting the shared judicial geography of northern Chile. However, the specific Iquique Court of Appeals annulment was delivered in Tarapacá, and Arica's own data contribution is limited to a 0.84 % share of national cases (2024). No trans-specific incident, court ruling, or enforcement failure originating in Arica was identified. The deviation below national rests on the shared northern judicial-climate framing and the broader pattern — reported for both the 2024 and 2025 Movilh annual surveys — that homo/transphobia cases rose in most regions outside the metropolitan core.

Against the national 0.72, this is a −0.03 deviation, the smallest in the scored set. Compared with Tarapacá (0.64), Arica is 0.05 higher because it lacks the concrete femicide-annulment ruling; the northern-court context applies but is not evidenced with a named local finding. Compared with Ñuble (0.67), Arica is 0.02 higher: Ñuble's +300 % surge is a more specific and dramatic statistical signal than Arica's sub-percent case share.

For a visitor, the practical exposure in Arica is not materially different from the national baseline; the small deduction reflects the dossier's explicit grouping under "worse than national" and the absence of any positive institutional finding (no diversity office, no municipal ordinance, no documented court protection).

records.name: RegiÃ³n Metropolitana de Santiago
records.summary:
Metropolitana is the region of best and worst in the country compressed into one administrative unit. Ñuñoa approved the first municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Chile that explicitly prohibits hate speech, obliges non-discrimination clauses in municipal tenders and contracts, creates a communal seal for good practice, and requires anti-exclusion notices in municipal buildings — a genuinely first-in-country institutional protection for a visitor in that commune. Vitacura's mayor declined to raise the LGBT pride flag on 17 May after a rebellion by Republican councillors, despite a prior commitment to Movilh. The ADM1 unit's internal spread (Ñuñoa vs Vitacura) is larger than most regions' entire deviation from the national score.

Metropolitana held 25.12 % of national cases in 2024 (second only to Valparaíso), but as the country's most populous region this share is roughly proportional. In 2025, Metropolitana was one of only two regions where recorded cases fell. The unit carries the strongest institutional depth in Chile: national-level courts, the largest civil-society infrastructure, the greatest concentration of trans and non-binary community resources, and the highest density of legal aid and complaint mechanisms available to a visitor who encounters discrimination.
